newsitem.title: USA: Report says Texas separatist leader to surrender.
newsitem.headline: Report says Texas separatist leader to surrender.

text.p: A Houston television station said on Wednesday the leader of an armed separatist group in Texas had agreed to surrender to end a four-day standoff with police, but officials would not confirm or deny the report.

Television station KPRC-TV said Richard McLaren, head of the Republic of Texas group, and his wife would be taken to a federal courthouse in Alpine, Texas where he would argue that he was a foreign diplomat not bound by U.S. laws.
The news report cited unnamed sources and it was unclear if the other 11 people holed up in a west Texas compound with McLaren were also involved in the agreement.
Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) spokesman Mike Cox said on Wednesday any discussion of surrender was "a rumour, pure speculation." He refused further comment.
Cox said on Tuesday negotiations between police and McLaren were going well and lawyer Terence O'Rourke told reporters he was seeking a day in court for his client.
"I am in the process of obtaining a hearing for him so that he doesn't have to die, but can argue his case in court. It's a very difficult stage we're in right now," he said.
But McLaren, in phone calls to the media on Tuesday, struck a belligerent tone and said, "We are in a state of war." He said his demands included "full diplomatic immunity."
O'Rourke did not speak to reporters on Wednesday as he entered the DPS command centre to continue negotiations.
The television station said it did not know when McLaren would surrender and indicated later it was possible he might not stand by the agreement.

The Republic of Texas, which was formed in 1995, advocates the secession of Texas from the United States. It claims to have thousands of members and links to anti-goverment militia groups around the country.
The standoff began on Sunday when Republic members took two hostages in retaliation for the arrest of its security chief, Robert Scheidt.

The hostages, who were seized from their home in a hail of bullets, were later released in exchange for Scheidt, but police filed felony charges against six Republic members that carry a maximum penalty of 99 years in prison.

Earlier on Wednesday, Texas Rangers detained seven men at a truck stop in Pecos, Texas after local police reported seeing a suspicous vehicle. News reports said the men may have been on their way to Fort Davis to join the Republic members.
DPS spokeswoman Sherri Deatherage Green said fully automatic weapons were found in two cars the men were using.

On Tuesday, the DPS said a bulletin had been issued warning that three men from a California-based militia may be headed to Fort Davis to help the Republic of Texas group, but it was not clear if these were the same suspects.
